newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia 97 oil exports seen steady after jump in 96.
newsitem.headline: Russia 97 oil exports seen steady after jump in 96.

text.p: High world oil prices last year prompted a surge in Russian crude oil exports, but capacity constraints in the country's export infrastructure could prevent a big export rise in 1997, oil analysts said on Tuesday.
State Statistics Committee data quoted by Interfax news agency put 1996 Russian oil exports at 105 million tonnes (2.1 million barrels per day), up nine percent from 1995 levels.
Including deliveries to the Commonwealth of Independent States, exports in 1996 hit 126 million tonnes (2.5 million bpd), up a more modest three percent from the year before.
Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of oil and gas at MC Securities Ltd in London, said a gap between Russian and foreign oil prices had grown along with Russian exports.
"Russian domestic oil prices have always been lower than international levels -- it's just that recently the disparity has grown," he said.
Russian 1996 oil exports rose despite a production drop -- 1996 output fell two percent on 1995 to 293 million tonnes (around 5.86 million bpd), the lowest level for nearly three decades.
Analysts said internal economic and political factors, as well as high world prices, were behind the rise in exports.
More favourable tax conditions for exporters in Russia encouraged deliveries to the West, they said.

"There was more of an incentive for Russian oil producers to export aggressively in the second half of 1996 than there was in the first as world crude prices were higher and export taxes eliminated," said James Bunch of Renaissance Capital in Moscow.
"Also, by exporting to world markets it means you usually get paid, whereas domestic sales are dogged by the non-payment crisis," he added.
And with Russia's pipeline systen still a government-owned entity, it would have been in Moscow's interest to raise as much cash from oil exports as possible, analysts said.
The relationship between domestic and international oil prices in 1997 will be a major factor determining export levels, analysts said.

But while world prices are trending lower, and at just over $21 a barrel are well down on the six-year high of $25 seen in October last year, the outlook for domestic Russian prices is not bullish either, they said.
"I think that domestic Russian prices of crude will not rise significantly this year from 1996," O'Sullivan said.
Russian demand for crude was unlikely to pick up soon as the country continued to struggle to reverse the steady decline in gross domestic product witnessed during the 1990s, he added.

Bunch said domestic oil use was partly constrained by an outdated refining industry, which meant that Russian plants were unable to cash in on producing more high-value, light-end products, and thereby consuming more crude oil.

The incentive to export big volumes were seen continuing in 1997 and possibly beyond, but constraints to the amount of oil the existing transport infrastructure could pump would prevent another big jump in exports in 1997, analysts said.
"One factor is the capacity of existing pipelines and export routes," said Mark Redway of T. Hoare and Co in London.
"Russia was certainly coming up against pipeline export constraints in 1996," O'Sullivan added.

Plans to increase export capacity from former Soviet Union (FSU) regions in the Caspian and Baltic could eventually boost FSU exports, but most of the projects were some way off completion, analysts said.
